document.summary: Total protein and 23 amino acids (19 protein-bound, 4 non-protein) were measured by wet chemistry in seeds of 206 sequenced EMS mutant lines of the reference line BTx623, grown at Lubbock, Texas in 2017. All mutants had higher protein than BTx623 (10.28-19.01% vs 10.35%), the best (ARS197) almost doubling it. Amino acids per seed weight rose with protein, but relative to protein several essential amino acids including lysine fell as protein rose. Five lines were also profiled by NIR for vitreosity, starch and amylose.
key_findings: Total protein of 206 EMS mutant lines ranged from 10.28% to 19.01%, all above wild-type BTx623 (10.35%).
ARS197 (19.14%), ARS152 (18.45%) and another line (18.04%) had 74-85% more protein than BTx623.
On a seed basis every amino acid increased with total protein; lysine showed the strongest relationship (R2 = 0.918), then threonine (0.746) and valine (0.720).

Relative to protein, lysine, threonine, methionine, histidine, tryptophan and other amino acids were negatively correlated with total protein, while glutamic acid, alanine and leucine were positively correlated.
ARS197 had about 89% more protein than BTx623 but lower lysine per protein (2.16 vs 2.39 g/100 g protein).
ARS158 and ARS125 had nearly double the histidine of BTx623 (0.41 vs 0.22 g/100 g seed).
In wild-type BTx623 protein, glutamic acid (21.11%), leucine (13.40%), alanine (9.34%) and proline (8.21%) were most abundant.
NIR protein agreed with wet chemistry (r = 0.857); ARS239 had the highest NIR protein (12.37%) and 26.7% less amylose than BTx623.

claims.subject: kafirin
claims.statement: Low essential amino acid levels and digestibility of sorghum are influenced by kafirin composition.
claims.context: sorghum grain; general statement
claims.evidence: Low essential amino acid levels and digestibility are inﬂuenced by the composition of the sorghum seed storage proteins, kaﬁrins.

claims.subject: kafirin
claims.statement: Kafirins are the sorghum prolamins, mostly located in spherical protein bodies of the endosperm.
claims.context: sorghum endosperm
claims.evidence: The most prevalent proteins, prolamins (kaﬁrins in sorghum), are present in the endosperm with the majority found in spherical protein bodies [10].

claims.subject: protein body
claims.statement: Most kafirin is located in spherical protein bodies in the endosperm.
claims.context: sorghum endosperm
claims.evidence: The most prevalent proteins, prolamins (kaﬁrins in sorghum), are present in the endosperm with the majority found in spherical protein bodies [10].

claims.subject: protein-starch matrix
claims.statement: Protein bodies and matrix protein form a barrier around starch granules that inhibits amylolytic hydrolysis of native and processed starch.
claims.context: sorghum endosperm; literature
claims.evidence: The combination of protein bodies and matrix protein in the endosperm forms a protein barrier around the starch granules, which in turn inhibits amylolytic enzymes from hydrolyzing native and processed starch [16,17].

claims.subject: kafirin polymerization
claims.statement: Polymerization of kafirins reduces protein digestibility.
claims.context: sorghum; literature
claims.evidence: Polymerization of kafirins results in reduced protein digestibility [23].

claims.subject: opaque2 maize
claims.statement: The maize opaque-2 mutant increases lysine and tryptophan levels.
claims.context: maize; literature
claims.evidence: For example, the opaque-2 mutant is a potential candidate for enhancing the maize protein quality by increasing its lysine and tryptophan levels [19].

claims.subject: HT12

claims.context: transgenic sorghum; literature

claims.subject: EMS mutagenesis
claims.statement: Total protein ranging from 10.28% to 19.01% across 206 mutant lines indicated new genetic variability from induced mutagenesis.
claims.context: 206 EMS mutant lines of BTx623
claims.evidence: Total protein content (10.28–19.01%) in 206 accessions indicated new genetic variability due to induced mutagenesis (Figure 1A).

claims.evidence: ARS197 (19.14%), ARS152 (18.45%), and ARS (18.04%) showed increases in total protein content of 84.92, 78.26, and 74.29%, respectively (Figure 1A).
